case_info.scenario: A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

[Case]
A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

Case:
A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

  B. Treat with carbamazepine

If they do not, we can then pivot to consider a more comprehensive evaluation of the lower motor neuron signs and their potential causes.

How do you reconcile treating with an anti-cholinesterase for what appears to be a hyperexcitable or spastic phenomenon, not a fatigable one?

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.
